To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the failure of economic institutions under the disaster situation of Hurricane Katrina was the failure of the neoliberalist policies that fostered the collapse of those institutions and the failure of the institutions to provide social provisioning for the most vulnerable members of the community.
the economic institutions in New Orleans were not designed or maintained to deal effectively with the flooding caused by Hurricane Katrina.
1) Hurricane Katrina represented a "perfect storm."
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how the collapse of basic economic institutions, in particular those that support the social provisioning process, can be avoided.
how economic institutions under the short-run policies failed to provide the social provisioning necessary for survival.
the role of institutions in the process of social production and provisioning.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the economic institutions of the United States failed miserably during the disaster of Hurricane Katrina.
the failure to provide for the basic needs of the poor in a disaster situation is a failure of the economic institutions of society.

the failure of the economic institutions was the result of the long run policies of growth over security, of the affluent and middle classes over the poor, of the market over the state, and of the private sector over the public sector.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
economic institutions, especially the institutions of the market, are critical to the process of social provision.
the neoliberalist philosophy and policies of privatization and deregulation, which were the basis of economic institutions, failed.
Hurricane Katrina revealed a failure in economic institutions, not just in the public sector, but also in the private sector.
The main takeaway from our work is that
economic institutions matter, and they matter in ways that are not obvious.
the collapse of basic economic institutions can be catastrophic for a community.
the economic institutions that support social provisioning are fragile and vulnerable to natural disasters and human-made disasters.
